evidence_items.source_text:
A man in his 30s presented with lower extremity sensory changes and falls. Three weeks before presentation, he noticed patchy, symmetric numbness and paresthesias in his legs and abdomen, just below the umbilicus. These sensory changes spared the upper trunk and arms. In the week preceding his presentation, he began experiencing what he described as weakness in his lower extremities and difficulty walking. He fell twice, injuring his ankle. He denied any sensory changes in his perineum or loss of bowel or bladder control. He reported normal diet without food restrictions and no gastrointestinal symptoms. He denied recent fevers or illnesses.
His past medical history was notable for Generalised Anxiety Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder, for which he was under the care of a therapist and psychiatrist and was prescribed fluoxetine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole. Previous lab reports showed intermittently borderline B12 levels (297 pg/mL, 300 pg/mL, 275 pg/mL) dating back 8 years, though he had never been formally diagnosed with a B12 deficiency. He reported using 450 canisters of nitrous oxide daily for the past 4–5 months. He drank three glasses of wine per week and smoked marijuana. He was not using any other illicit substances at the time of presentation.

Physical examination revealed absent vibratory sense in the lower extremities, impaired proprioception in a distal to proximal fashion (absent at the toes, diminished at the ankles), and diminished two-point discrimination in a distal to proximal fashion, noted in both the lower and upper extremities. In addition, the patient exhibited a superimposed patchy impairment in light touch sensation up to roughly the umbilicus and decreased pinprick sensation bilaterally to the mid-shins. Temperature sensation was preserved. He required one-person assist for sitting balance and two-person assist for walking, requiring a rolling walker to walk independently. His stance was wide-based, and there was a positive Romberg sign.
Reflexes were absent in the lower extremities and normal in the upper extremities. There was no response to plantar stimulation. Motor strength, mental status, cranial nerves and coordination were all intact.

MRI of the spinal cord revealed patchy hyperintense T2 spinal cord signal abnormality without enhancement in the cervical and thoracic spine, predominantly seen in the dorsal aspect of the cord, and extending from C3 to the T9-T10 disc level (figure 1). MRI brain was normal.

Laboratory testing demonstrated a normal haemoglobin level of 140 g/L (normal range 120–180 g/L) with macrocytosis (MCV 94 fL; 78–94 fL). Vitamin B12 level was normal (672; normal range 232–1245 pg/mL), but with elevated methylmalonic acid (5.86 µmol/L; normal range 0.00–0.40 µmol/L) and homocysteine levels (32 µmol/L; 4.0–15.0 µmol/L), and intrinsic factor blocking antibodies were present.

Gastric biopsy showed chronic inflammation and reactive changes in the antral and oxyntic mucosa, and duodenal biopsy showed peptic duodenitis and reactive epithelial cells. The biopsies were negative for giardia, coeliac disease and Helicobacter pylori immunostain.
The patient was diagnosed with subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and polyneuropathy secondary to concomitant nitrous oxide abuse and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

Nitrous oxide use impairs metabolism of vitamin B12, while atrophic gastritis impairs vitamin B12 absorption. In the case of the patient described above, a combination of impaired absorption and impaired metabolism precipitated subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.
